headline: Gelsinger-backed Nagare Labs’ Z2RAM promises SRAM speed at DRAM density for AI chips
summary: Nagare Labs' Z2RAM aims for 5x SRAM density and 14x DRAM speed with 3x less read energy than SRAM, stacking memory directly on AI chips.
details: Nagare Labs, a Georgia Tech spinout backed by Pat Gelsinger, has unveiled Z2RAM, a new memory technology. It promises SRAM-level speed at DRAM density, designed to be stacked directly onto AI chips.
The first generation of Z2RAM is projected to achieve 5x SRAM density using six stacked layers. It also boasts 14x DRAM speed and 3x less read energy than traditional SRAM.

AI chips demand immense memory bandwidth, and current high-bandwidth memory (HBM) solutions face challenges with yield and heat. Manufacturers often settle for fewer layers due to these issues, limiting performance.

Existing alternatives like high-bandwidth flash or stacked SRAM/DRAM have their own drawbacks. SRAM is less dense and more expensive for capacity, while DRAM stacking is limited by the heat generated by the underlying logic.

Nagare Labs describes Z2RAM as "Two transistors and a shield. No capacitor," allowing for non-destructive reads. This design avoids DRAM's refresh cycles by holding charge in the read transistor's gate capacitance.

Z2RAM is built by depositing layers directly on the accelerator and patterning them together on one die, similar to 3D NAND flash. This process uses standard 300mm tools with DUV, eliminating the need for expensive EUV lithography.

The technology's founders have demonstrated improved data retention, with cells holding data for over 300 seconds at 85°C in recent papers. While this is a significant improvement, it still needs to reach DRAM's typical 95°C operating threshold for full viability.
